analysis.one_liner: Toughens mine safety enforcement, raises penalties for violators, and strengthens protections for miners and other workers.
analysis.headline: Introduced 17 days before the 116th Congress ended with three Senate Democrats behind it, the bill went to the Senate health committee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the federal Mine Safety and Health Act to give safety regulators more power over coal and other mines: independent investigations of deadly accidents, higher civil fines and new felony charges for operators who knowingly violate safety rules, personal legal liability for company executives, stronger whistle-blower protections for miners who report hazards, and paid time when a safety order closes a mine. It also requires underground coal mines to install air-quality monitoring systems, brief miners on hazards before each shift, and use more rock dust to prevent explosions. A separate title extends workplace safety law (OSHA) to government employees and raises penalties across the board.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners, especially underground miners, gain stronger protections: independent investigations of deadly accidents, the right to refuse work they reasonably believe is dangerous without being fired, reinstatement with back pay if they are retaliated against, and pay while a safety order idles the mine. All workers, including government employees, gain from expanded OSHA coverage and whistle-blower rights. Families of killed or injured miners gain standing to participate in investigations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal miners, their families, and public employees

how_it_helps.text: Requires an independent investigation panel, with subpoena power, for any mine accident involving three or more deaths, and directs the panel to examine failures by the operator, contractors, and government agencies.

Makes knowingly violating mine safety standards a felony punishable by up to five years in prison and a $1 million fine, and puts the same civil and criminal liability on directors, officers, and agents who knowingly order or carry out violations.

Greatly expands whistle-blower protections, prohibits enforcement of pre-dispute arbitration waivers of those rights, and lets a miner who is retaliated against get immediate reinstatement, back pay, and attorney's fees.
Guarantees miners full pay for shifts lost when a safety withdrawal order closes a mine, up to 60 days for extended closures.

Requires underground coal mines to install atmospheric monitoring systems, raise rock dusting from 65% to 80% incombustible content, and orally brief each miner on hazardous conditions before the miner travels to the work area.
Extends Occupational Safety and Health Act coverage to government employees, raises OSHA's civil and criminal penalties, and adds victims' rights for workers injured or killed on the job.

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators, who would face sharply higher fines (up to $220,000 for targeted violations like unauthorized ventilation changes and skipped rock dusting), doubled penalties at mines with patterns of violations, personal liability for executives, felony exposure, and the cost of new monitoring equipment, certification fees, and communication programs. OSHA-regulated employers and government employers would bear higher penalties and, for public agencies, the cost of complying with federal workplace safety law for the first time.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mine operators and OSHA-covered employers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are substantial: operators must buy and install atmospheric monitoring systems, adopt direct-reading dust monitors, fund a personnel certification system through operator-paid fees, and run pre-shift communication programs.

Doubled penalties for mines with a pattern of violations and the threat of withdrawal orders that idle an entire mine could strain marginal operators, and some of that cost pressure could fall on coal jobs and coal-reliant communities.
Extending OSHA to every government employee nationwide is a major expansion that would impose new inspection, recordkeeping, and abatement costs on state and local governments and taxpayers.
The bill sets tight regulatory deadlines, including 180 days for several rulemakings, which regulators would struggle to meet properly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is money against life: the costs fall on mine operators and employers, while the protections address the reason miners die on the job, including exploded dust levels, disabled safety devices, and retaliation against miners who report hazards. The strongest good-faith objections are the compliance burden on smaller mines, the nationwide expansion of OSHA to public employees tacked onto a mine bill, and deadlines regulators likely could not meet. On balance, the safety provisions are aimed directly at practices that have historically killed miners, and the costs are ones an honest supporter would defend as the price of safe mines.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee in the final two weeks of the Congress and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Casey introduced the bill on December 17, 2020, joined by Senators Sherrod Brown and Joe Manchin as cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The committee took no further action, and the bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no House consideration before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators are better off because the bill died: no higher fines, no doubled pattern-of-violations penalties, no personal felony exposure for executives, and no new monitoring, rock dust, certification, or communication requirements. OSHA-regulated employers and government employers also avoided the expanded coverage and penalties in Title VII.

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-led Senate took no action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All three backers were Democrats and not a single Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill targets exactly the practices that have killed miners, including unauthorized ventilation changes, skipped rock dusting, disabling safety devices, and retaliation against miners who report hazards. Operators would pay up to $220,000 for targeted violations, doubled penalties at pattern-of-violations mines, and up to $2 million and 10 years in the worst repeat criminal cases, plus new equipment and certification costs.

OSHA coverage would extend to government employees for the first time, creating new compliance and abatement costs for public agencies. Their interest in avoiding the mandate runs against the public employees who would gain federal safety protections.

Higher civil and criminal penalties, victims' rights, expanded whistle-blower protection, and procedures to force correction of serious violations before contest would raise the cost of unsafe practices across covered industries.

Mandated atmospheric monitoring systems, direct-reading coal dust explosibility monitors, and electronic recordkeeping requirements would create a guaranteed market for monitoring and safety equipment sold to underground coal mines.
